title: Children in foster care give the most positive answers in Ofsted's 2026 survey
standfirst: Ofsted's annual questionnaire of children in care and residential settings found those living with foster carers were the most likely to say they feel safe, are listened to and had done something fun in the past week.
body: Ofsted has published the results of its 2026 children's social care questionnaires, the yearly online survey it sends to children and adults connected with children's homes, fostering and adoption services, supported accommodation, residential family centres, boarding schools, residential special schools and further education colleges with residential provision in England. The survey ran for seven weeks, from 2 February to 22 March 2026, and the report was published on 29 October.

Ofsted received 46,900 responses across all the groups it surveyed, of which 8,360 came from children, down from 8,880 in 2025. Across every setting, 96% of children said they feel safe where they live or stay, 91% said they feel listened to always or most of the time, and 77% said they spend time with people who are important to them.

Children living with foster carers stood out. Ofsted says they reported overwhelmingly positive experiences across all of its questions, and they were the group most likely to say they feel safe always, at 92%. Some 98% said the people looking after them listen to them always or most of the time, and 95% gave positive answers when asked whether they are asked about things that matter to them, the highest of any setting alongside supported accommodation.

Children in foster care were also the most likely to say they get on with the other children in the household, at 92%, up from 88% in 2025 and close to the 91% recorded in 2024. And 96% said they had done something fun in the previous week, the highest rate of any setting and unchanged for three years. The one area with more room to improve was time with important people: in Ofsted's tables, 53% of children in foster care said they always spend time with people who matter to them and 28% said most of the time.

Ofsted uses the answers, together with earlier inspection findings and other information, to decide when to inspect a service and what to focus on. Trained staff read responses as they arrive and pass any safeguarding concern straight to inspectors. The report notes that not every child in a fostering setting is looked after, as some are receiving short breaks. Answers from adults, including foster carers and kinship carers, are published separately as data rather than in the report.

For anyone thinking about fostering, the survey is a reminder of what carers are already giving children day to day: a safe home, someone who listens, and ordinary family life. Around two in three looked-after children in England live with foster carers, according to the report, and the government has set a goal of creating 10,000 more foster places over this Parliament. Ofsted runs the survey every year, so current carers whose fostering service is asked to take part can encourage the children they look after to have their say.

title: UK foster carer pay by council 2026-27: what 25 councils publish
standfirst: Weekly allowances in the 25 councils we have checked run from £176 for a baby to £337.40 for a teenager, and the fees paid to carers on top vary even more.
body: Fostering Today has now published the 2026-27 foster carer allowances for 25 UK councils, each taken from the council's own website, committee papers or rate schedules and linked to that source on our council pages. Twenty of the councils are in England and five in Scotland. This summary brings those pages together so prospective carers, current carers and anyone writing about fostering can compare what councils say they pay. We will update it as more councils are added.

The weekly allowance is the money paid for each child's day-to-day costs, and it rises with age. Across the 23 councils that publish it as a separate figure, the lowest rate for the youngest age band is £176 a week, paid by Calderdale and Northumberland for children up to two, and the highest is £210 a week, paid by Kent for children under two. For the oldest children, seven councils (Calderdale, Leicester, Newcastle, Northumberland, Rochdale, Wakefield and Walsall) pay £267 a week and Staffordshire pays £267.50, while Coventry pays £337.40 and Lincolnshire £331.66 for young people aged 16 and over. The gap between £267 and £337.40 is £70.40 a week for a teenager in the same age band, or £3,660.80 over a year.

Two councils publish a single weekly total that combines the child's allowance with the carer's reward or professional fee instead of listing them separately. Bracknell Forest's Tier 1 totals run from £304.83 to £480.34 a week depending on the child's age, and Thurrock's from £415 to £516 at its standard Care Skills rate and up to £568 at Care Skills+.

In Scotland, East Ayrshire, Highland, Scottish Borders and Shetland all publish the same three allowance rates, £177.68, £206.71 and £283.35 a week, which Shetland's page notes match the Scottish Recommended Allowance for the year. Aberdeenshire pays more in every age band, from £191.13 to £307.79 a week.

Fees are where councils differ most. Nineteen of the 25 publish a weekly fee, skills or reward payment for mainstream carers on top of the allowance; two publish combined totals; Aberdeenshire pays an annual skills payment starting at £10,431.21 for newly approved carers; Highland's schedule shows fees only for specialist and intensive carers; and the pages for Lincolnshire and Shetland list no fee. Starting levels vary widely: Leicester's Level 1 payment for newly approved carers is £50 a week per child, Wakefield's Skill Level 1 is £53 and Central Bedfordshire's first tier is £100, while Croydon's entry-level skills fee is £325 a week. Several councils, including Bristol and Staffordshire, pay no fee at their first level.

Each council's page on Fostering Today shows its full age bands, fee levels and extras such as birthday, holiday and festival payments, with the date we checked it. Age bands and fee structures are not the same from one council to the next, so the fairest comparison is the full table for the area you live in, and the fostering team can confirm what would apply to you. Our pay calculator puts council and agency figures side by side.

title: Welsh councils must send first care sufficiency plans by 1 December as new rules take effect
standfirst: Regulations requiring every Welsh council to publish an annual plan for finding enough local homes for children in care, including foster homes, came into force on 26 October 2026.
body: New regulations requiring local authorities in Wales to prepare annual sufficiency plans for the children they look after came into force on 26 October 2026. On the same day the Welsh Government published guidance and a template for councils to use, setting out what the plans must cover and how they will be approved, submitted and revised.

According to the Welsh Government's November newsletter on removing profit from children's care, each plan will assess the current and future care and accommodation needs of the children a council looks after and explain how it will secure enough suitable places for them. The regulations list the information every plan has to contain. Councils must send their first drafts to Welsh Ministers by 1 December 2026 and publish them, once approved, by 31 March 2027.

The plans are part of Wales's wider move, under the Health and Social Care (Wales) Act 2025, to a not-for-profit model for children's homes, fostering and secure accommodation. The newsletter repeats that from 1 April 2027 existing for-profit providers will not be able to approve new foster carers or add beds unless they have re-established as a not-for-profit body, and says Care Inspectorate Wales is updating its FAQs and contacting independent fostering services directly. The Welsh Government expects to publish its response to the consultation on limiting further for-profit growth this month.

The newsletter also reports two developments aimed at carers. Foster Wales, through which all 22 Welsh councils work together, launched a new Learning and Development Framework in September 2026, with new modules, a digital e-book and an online portal, and showcased it at its annual conference in Llangollen on 23 September. Separately, ADSS Cymru, the body representing social services directors, has worked with Foster Wales on a national fostering cost model, a framework for understanding the costs of recruiting, approving and supporting foster carers.

What this means for you: sufficiency plans are where councils set out how many and what kind of placements they expect to need, so the published plans should show where demand for local foster carers is greatest, for example for teenagers or sibling groups. If you are thinking about fostering in Wales, your council's fostering team, working as part of Foster Wales, remains the main route in alongside not-for-profit agencies. Foster Wales says its councils are working together to help foster carers who want to transfer from for-profit agencies.

What happens next: draft plans go to Welsh Ministers by 1 December, the consultation response on the 2027 restrictions is due in November, and approved plans must be published by the end of March 2027. ADSS Cymru is holding an online briefing on the changes on 12 January 2027. We will report the consultation outcome when it is published.

title: Six north London councils launch a shared fostering hub led by Camden
standfirst: Barnet, Camden, Enfield, Hackney, Haringey and Islington have officially launched the North London Fostering Hub to recruit, support and keep foster carers across the six boroughs.
body: Six councils in north London have officially launched a joint fostering hub, Camden Council announced on 5 November 2026. The North London Fostering Hub brings together Barnet, Camden, Enfield, Hackney, Haringey and Islington, with Camden acting as the lead authority. The partnership will recruit, support and retain foster carers across the area so that more children in care can live with families close to their schools, friends and communities.

The hub is part of the government’s national fostering reform programme in England. Camden’s fostering service had earlier said that the government confirmed 14 fostering hubs would be operating across England from this autumn, and that the north London hub would build on the North London Fostering and Permanency Consortium, through which the same six councils have worked together since 2012. Camden describes the new hub as building on more than a decade of that collaboration.

According to the council, the hub is designed to make three stages easier: finding out about fostering in the first place, getting support while an application goes through, and receiving training and guidance once someone has been approved as a foster carer. Camden’s fostering pages also say that Room Makers, a scheme that funds changes to foster carers’ homes to create extra space, is being expanded to all fostering hubs.

The launch coincided with the first national gathering of regional fostering hubs, which Camden hosted this week. Representatives from hubs across England attended, along with the Minister for Children and Families, Josh MacAlister, to share learning and discuss how regional partnerships can strengthen fostering services. The minister said fostering changes lives and described the national recruitment campaign as opening fostering up to ordinary people across England. Councillor Marcus Boyland, Camden’s Cabinet Member for Best Start for Children and Families, said that joining forces across six boroughs would help the councils reach more people considering fostering and better support existing carers.

For anyone in north London thinking about fostering, the practical change is a single front door covering six boroughs rather than six separate routes. Camden says people from all backgrounds are encouraged to apply, and that fostering can fit alongside different careers and lifestyles; its fostering pages note that people who are single, married, in a relationship, working or retired may be able to foster. Enquiries go through the hub’s website, fosternorthlondon.gov.uk.

Regional hubs are one of the ways the government hopes to increase the number of fostering households in England. Prospective carers elsewhere can check whether their own council belongs to a hub, and can compare council and agency fostering services in their area on Fostering Today.

title: Private Fostering Awareness Day 2026: councils remind families caring for someone else's child to tell them
standfirst: Councils marked Private Fostering Awareness Day on 4 November by reminding parents and carers that arrangements lasting 28 days or more must be reported, as CoramBAAF published new findings from 48 local authorities.
body: CoramBAAF held its annual Private Fostering Awareness Day on Wednesday 4 November 2026, the first Wednesday in November. The day aims to raise awareness of children who live with someone other than a parent or close relative by private agreement, a group CoramBAAF describes as often overlooked. Alongside the day it published a new report, Private Fostering Report 2026: findings and analysis, which brings together information from 48 local authorities.

Private fostering is different from the fostering most people know. It is an arrangement made privately between a parent and another adult, without the council placing the child, for a child under 16 (under 18 if disabled) who is looked after by someone who is not a parent or close relative, and where the arrangement is meant to last at least 28 days. Close relatives are grandparents, aunts and uncles, brothers and sisters, and step-parents; a cousin, great-aunt or family friend caring for a child would usually count as a private foster carer. Councils give examples such as a parent going into hospital, a teenager moving in with a friend's family after a family breakdown, or a young person from overseas staying with a host family to study.

CoramBAAF points out that national data collection on private fostering stopped in 2015, so there has been limited insight into how many children live in these arrangements and what they look like. Its survey of councils is one of the few ways of filling that gap.

Councils used the day to remind residents of the law. Somerset Council said parents and private foster carers have a legal responsibility to tell the council, and Knowsley said notification is a legal requirement and asked anyone about to start an arrangement to contact its safeguarding hub before it begins. In England, the Children (Private Arrangements for Fostering) Regulations 2005 say a proposed private foster carer should notify the council at least six weeks before the arrangement starts, or immediately if it is due to start sooner. The council must then arrange a visit within seven working days to see the carer, the household and the child, and keep visiting regularly while the arrangement lasts.

What this means for you: if you are looking after a friend's or a more distant relative's child for four weeks or more, or are about to, contact the children's services team at your local council. Notifying is about making sure the child is safe and that you can get advice and support; Somerset and Gloucestershire both describe the help on offer to private foster carers. Private fostering is not the same as becoming an approved foster carer through a council or agency, which involves a full assessment and fostering allowances. If caring for a child has made you think about fostering more widely, our guides explain how that process works.

What happens next: CoramBAAF's 2026 report and awareness materials are available on its website for councils and professionals. The 2005 regulations apply in England, so families in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland should check the rules with their local council or health and social care trust.

title: Wales sets out rules to carry foster carer approvals over when agencies go not-for-profit
standfirst: Welsh Government impact assessments published on 10 November describe new regulations letting carers keep their approval when a for-profit fostering service re-forms as a not-for-profit body, instead of being assessed again.
body: The Welsh Government has published four impact assessments for the Fostering Panels (Establishment and Functions) (Wales) (Amendment and Transitional Provision) Regulations 2026, all dated 10 November 2026. They cover the integrated, children's rights, equality and Welsh language impacts of a change designed to keep foster carer approvals in place while fostering services move to a not-for-profit model.

The background is the Health and Social Care (Wales) Act 2025, which removes profit from children's residential care, secure accommodation and fostering. The integrated assessment says the aim is for this care to be largely delivered by not-for-profit providers registered with Care Inspectorate Wales (CIW) by 2030. The difficulty it identifies is that when a for-profit fostering service re-establishes itself as a not-for-profit organisation, it becomes a new legal entity. Approvals cannot simply move across, and a carer cannot be approved by two agencies at the same time, so without a change every carer would face full re-approval: a fresh suitability assessment, updated checks and references, a fostering panel and a new agency decision.

The regulations amend the Fostering Panels (Establishment and Functions) (Wales) Regulations 2018 so that, in strictly defined and time-limited circumstances, existing approvals transfer automatically to the new not-for-profit body where there is clear organisational and operational continuity. Safeguards listed include checks that the transfer is valid, continued supervision of carers, a mandatory review of each transferred approval within 12 months, CIW oversight and national guidance. The children's rights assessment refers to a proposed sunset provision, meaning the arrangement is meant to be temporary.

According to the integrated assessment, a 12-week public consultation showed broad support, with respondents stressing placement stability, safeguarding oversight and clear, consistent guidance. Those taking part included foster carers, for-profit and not-for-profit providers, councils, CIW, sector bodies and the Children's Commissioner for Wales. The assessment gives a start date of December 2026 and says the regulations follow the negative procedure in the Senedd. It does not give an exact date, and the regulations themselves had not appeared on legislation.gov.uk when we checked.

What this means for you: if you foster in Wales with a for-profit agency that plans to become a charity or other not-for-profit body, the aim is that you keep your approval and your placements without starting the assessment again, though your approval would be reviewed within a year of the transfer. If you are thinking about fostering in Wales, councils working together as Foster Wales and not-for-profit agencies are the routes the system is moving towards. We will report the final regulations and their in-force date when they are published.

title: Government plan aims to halve homelessness among young people leaving care in England
standfirst: A Care Leaver Homelessness Reduction Action Plan published on 5 November sets two national targets, new duties on councils and fresh guidance, including on young people who stay with their foster carers after 18.
body: The Department for Education and the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government published the Care Leaver Homelessness Reduction Action Plan on 5 November 2026, at the start of Care Leavers Month. It applies to England and sets two targets to be met by the end of this Parliament: that no young person becomes homeless when leaving care, and that the proportion of care leavers under 25 experiencing homelessness is halved.

According to the government's announcement, the number of care leavers aged 18 to 24 in England has risen to 86,890, up almost 10% in two years. Under the plan, councils will have to publish plans for how they will meet care leavers' accommodation needs, work with housing partners, and set out in their local offer the support available to young people at risk of homelessness. Councils are also encouraged to publish local targets, and areas at higher risk will get targeted support overseen by MHCLG youth homelessness advisers.

The plan builds on changes made by the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act this year. The government says certain care leavers under 25 can no longer be found intentionally homeless, and that care leavers no longer have to meet local connection tests to get social housing. Alongside the plan come a guide called Planning Housing Pathways for Care Leavers, updated joint guidance for housing and children's services, a youth homelessness prevention toolkit, a new youth chapter in the Homelessness Code of Guidance and a £3m Test, Learn, Grow programme focused on preventing youth homelessness. Updated social housing allocations guidance is due in 2027.

For foster carers, the most direct item is new guidance on young people who stay with their foster carers after 18. The announcement also says Staying Close, which supports young people leaving residential care, is already running in 50 areas and will become a national duty on councils for care leavers up to 25 from 2029, and that from autumn 2027 government departments and public bodies will also become corporate parents.

The charity Become welcomed the national targets and the new duties on councils, but called for care leavers to be given greater priority for social housing and for consistent training for the personal advisers who support them. Its chief executive said care leavers are nine times more likely to face homelessness than other young people.

For anyone thinking about fostering, the plan is a reminder that a fostering relationship does not have to end at 18. Many young people can stay on with their foster family into early adulthood, and the quality of support around that move matters. If you are considering fostering older children or teenagers, ask the services you speak to how they support young people and carers when a placement reaches 18, and what the council's local offer for care leavers includes.
